newsitem.title: INDIA: Mother Teresa's illness highlights succession.
newsitem.headline: Mother Teresa's illness highlights succession.

text.p: Mother Teresa's heart problems have thrust into focus the issue of who will lead her worldwide Roman Catholic order devoted to the poor if she retires or dies.
It is something that most of the 4,500 or so nuns in her Missionaries of Charity, spread across 111 countries, do not want to contemplate.
Mother Teresa, 86, founded the Calcutta-based order in 1948 and has led it since then with charisma.
She underwent life-saving surgery in a Calcutta clinic on Friday to unblock two coronary arteries. On Sunday, she was reported to be stable but with an irregular heart rhythm.
"It is God's wish that Mother Teresa should continue to lead His work of love for the poorest of poor," Sister Priscilla Lewis, the order's spokeswoman, told Reuters on Saturday.
She declined comment on reports that the 1979 Nobel Peace laureate might seek Vatican consent to retire at any time.
Mother Teresa, affectionately known as "Mother" to her nuns and to many people in predominantly Hindu India, was fitted with a heart pacemaker in 1989.
"There is no problem over a successor to the Mother. We have been upset over the Mother's health. We have been praying for her recovery," she added.
But a charity source, who asked not to be named, said: "Mother Teresa does not want to continue as superior general because of her poor health and a weak heart.
"Even in 1990, she wanted to step down because of ill health. But she was forced to stay as superior general as a suitable replacement could not be found," the source said.
Sources close to the charity say there are several potential candidates to replace her, if necessary, as superior general in a regular six-year election by secret ballot set for January.
The poll was delayed from September 8 when Mother Teresa was previously in hospital with heart problems, pneumonia and malaria.
"Mother believes in free democratic elections in her organisation. But she may be in favour of a pre-election consensus to choose her successor," Sister Priscilla said.
The order's constitution says if the superior general dies or is unable to perform her duties, the assistant general will take over, pending a fresh election within 90 days.
Maltese-born Sister Frederica, in her 60s, is the current assistant general, or second-in-charge.
Apart from a superior general, a four-member council, including an assistant general, is also elected.
The charity voted for the first time in 1961.
The election process begins with forming an electoral college, mainly with representatives from various sections of the order, including the regions, postulants and novices.
The college, or General Chapter, meeting is preceded by a one-week retreat to allow its 103 members "to communicate with God and vote according to God's will".
Sister Frederica, the assistant general, was a former regional supervisor of the order in the United States.
In 1990, she replaced Sister Agnes Das, a Bengali nun and Mother Teresa's first disciple in the charity.
Mother Teresa has described Sister Agnes as her "second self". In 1990, when Mother Teresa wanted to step down, Agnes withdrew from the electoral scene on medical grounds.
India's Asian Age newspaper said last week a potential superior general appeared to be Hindu-born Sister Nirmala, who heads the orders Comtemplative Wing of "elite" nuns.
Sister Priscilla, as well as Sisters Joseph Michael and Monica, are all from Bengal and members of the order's council.
The Missionaries of Charity has 456 centres in 111 countries. It feeds 500,000 families each year, teaches 20,000 children in its schools and treats 90,000 lepers in its clinics.
It also runs orphanages and other homes for the dying.
